opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is really the heart of it. If you train a weather model with a standard deterministic loss like mean squared error, you're asking it to predict the conditional mean. In a chaotic system, that mean gets blurrier the further out you go. You get forecasts that look smooth and score well on RMSE, but they're physically unrealistic. They lose the small-scale structure, the extremes get washed out, and you can't really use them to reason about risk.

So if the goal is ensemble prediction, the objective has to say that directly. You want the model to learn the *distribution* of possible future states, not a single best guess. That means moving toward proper scoring rules, with something like the continuous ranked probability score as the natural choice. A proper scoring rule rewards you for being calibrated: your spread should match your actual error, and each individual member should still look like a plausible atmosphere.

A few things matter in practice. First, the model has to be stochastic in a meaningful way. You inject noise, ideally structured noise that respects the geometry of the sphere and has realistic correlations across scales, so different members actually diverge in physically sensible ways rather than just jittering. Second, you evaluate the loss over the ensemble jointly, not member by member, so the model is penalized both for being wrong on average and for being over- or under-dispersive. Third, you care about spectral fidelity. A good probabilistic model should preserve the energy spectrum across wavelengths, so you're not quietly smoothing away the small scales the way deterministic models do.

There's also a nice computational argument. Traditional ensemble systems are extremely expensive, which is why operational centers can only run tens of members. If a learned model is trained properly as a generative, probabilistic forecaster, you can produce very large ensembles cheaply. That opens the door to better characterizing tail events, like heat waves, extreme precipitation, and hurricane tracks, which is ultimately what decision makers care about.

So the short version is: the training objective should match how the forecast will be used. If people will consume it as an ensemble to quantify uncertainty, you should train it to be a calibrated, physically consistent sampler of the future, not a regressor toward the mean.

r001.rationale: It says the objective should train the model to predict the distribution of future states and use proper scoring rules that reward calibration, directly tying objective accuracy to ensemble prediction.

fable-5.1.text:
The short answer is that if the goal is an ensemble, you cannot train the model as if the goal were a single best guess. That sounds obvious, but it was the mistake baked into the first generation of these models, including our own earlier versions of FourCastNet.

When you train with a mean squared error loss on a deterministic prediction, the model is rewarded for producing the conditional mean. For weather, the conditional mean at five or ten days out is a blurry, washed-out field. It's a terrible sample of the atmosphere. It has no sharp fronts, no realistic storm structure, and if you perturb the inputs and run it as an ensemble, the members collapse toward each other because the network has learned to hedge rather than to commit to physically plausible outcomes. So you get an ensemble that is underdispersed and overconfident, which is exactly the failure mode you don't want in an operational setting.

So in FourCastNet 3 we made the objective itself probabilistic. The model is trained directly on a proper scoring rule, the continuous ranked probability score, computed across the ensemble members during training. A proper score only has its optimum when the predicted distribution matches the true distribution, so the model is rewarded both for being accurate and for having the right spread. We also account for spatial correlation in that score, because you don't want a model that gets the marginal distribution at each grid point right but produces fields that are spatially incoherent. Weather is a field, not a collection of independent pixels.

The other piece that matters is where the stochasticity comes from. Classical ensembles get it from perturbing initial conditions and model physics. In our case the noise is injected into the network itself, and we were careful that it respects the geometry of the sphere, so the perturbations don't have artifacts at the poles or along seams. Training with the probabilistic loss then teaches the model how to use that noise, in the sense that it learns the structure of uncertainty rather than just adding random jitter.

And this connects to the longer-horizon goal. If you want stable rollouts out to weeks or even seasonal scales, and you want to study things like extremes and tail events, the model has to represent a distribution that's physically faithful, with the right spectral content, rather than a smooth average. Getting the training objective right is really what unlocks that. It's a case where the loss function is not a detail of engineering, it's the statement of what you actually want the model to be.

r001.rationale: The response says FourCastNet 3 is trained with a probabilistic CRPS objective across ensemble members, rewarding accuracy and the right spread so the predicted distribution matches the true distribution.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that you’re trying to learn a distribution of possible futures, rather than just one best forecast. If you train every ensemble member with a pointwise mean-squared error against the same observation, you encourage them all to converge toward the conditional mean. You can get a reasonable average forecast, but you lose the diversity that makes an ensemble useful.

So the training objective needs to reward both accuracy and calibration. The ensemble should be concentrated when the future is predictable and spread out when there’s real uncertainty. A proper probabilistic scoring rule can help capture that balance: you don’t get rewarded simply for adding more spread.

And for weather, those samples need to be coherent across space and time. It’s not enough to get the uncertainty right at each individual location if the resulting weather patterns aren’t physically meaningful. So I would want the objective—and the evaluation—to reflect the quality of the whole predictive distribution, including its behavior over longer rollouts and for extreme events.

r001.rationale: The response says the objective should reward accuracy and calibration of the ensemble’s predictive distribution, supporting ensemble prediction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that the training objective has to reward predicting the distribution of possible futures, rather than just predicting one trajectory accurately. If you train only with a mean squared error objective, you tend to get something close to the conditional mean, which can smooth out the extremes and underrepresent uncertainty.

For ensemble prediction, you want both calibration and sharpness: the ensemble should have enough spread to capture what actually happens, but it shouldn’t be unnecessarily broad. So the objective needs to evaluate the ensemble as a whole, using a proper probabilistic scoring rule. Diversity by itself isn’t the goal—it has to reflect the uncertainty in the system. And for weather, that uncertainty needs to remain physically coherent across space, across variables, and over time.

r001.rationale: The response says the objective should reward predicting the distribution of possible futures and evaluate the ensemble with a proper probabilistic scoring rule, directly targeting probabilistic prediction accuracy for ensemble prediction.
